posts.text: A father's courage

quoted.text:
A 5-year-old girl plunged 49 feet from a moving cruise ship into the open ocean. Her father heard his wife screaming and raced toward the railing, only to discover that their daughter was gone.

It happened aboard the Disney Dream near the Bahamas, where a family vacation took a terrifying turn when the little girl fell from the ship’s fourth deck.

When her father realized what had happened, he jumped overboard after her, plunging nearly 50 feet into the ocean. But when he surfaced, he couldn’t see his daughter anywhere.

He began desperately calling out for her, searching the water until he finally heard her calling back. He swam toward her and managed to reach her, but they were still stranded in the open ocean as the massive cruise ship began turning around.

For roughly 20 minutes, he kept his little girl afloat, holding her above the water until a rescue boat finally reached them and brought them back to safety.

Both survived, although the father suffered two fractures in his spine from the fall.

It takes an incredible amount of courage to jump nearly 50 feet into the open ocean, not knowing what awaits you below. But this father didn’t hesitate to put his own life on the line for his little girl. Thank God they both made it home.

After US CPI inflation rose to 3.7% on Wednesday, the 10Y Note Yield surged to 5.33%.

It appears that if the risks/ capabilities demand, a filing regime or prohibition may be considered, but this will be narrowly enforced and affect only a small number of products & services. 

So, what hasn't changed: Open model releases at home and abroad remain a welcomed development by the government. 

What has been clarified: On the open weight AI front, expect China to step up capability/risk-based governance to meet domestic needs, global demands.

1. 此次修订亦是技术贸易管理的**常态化⼯作**，依法依规进⾏，不针对任何特定国家、地区或实体。

⼼政务等敏感系统，或⽤于绕过国家安全防御体系**。
6. ⿎励开源开放、合作共享。... **为⽀持构建⼈⼯智能开源创新⽣态体系，对⼈⼯智能类技术开源、中国企业在境外⾃建⾃营算⼒中⼼、赴境外开展芯⽚流⽚制造、利⽤境外资源开展联合研发、参与国际标准制定等情形的技术出，适⽤⾃动许可等便利措施，基本实现“即报即出”** ；对已通过开源、发表学术论⽂等⽅式进⼊公共领域的相关技术，拟不纳⼊出⼝管理范围，为⼈⼯智能技术国际交流合作创造良好环。

You guys know I have been interested in the rural health transformation efforts and whether things will be truly transformational.

Well, CMS just dropped its first obligated funds report for the Rural Health Transformation Program, showing how each state has obligated RHTP funds (as reported by the states themselves) between December 29, 2025 through July 31, 2026. 

Year One officially closes on October 30 so there's more reporting to come. CMS plans to refresh the numbers once states submit their November 30 quarterly reports, then quarterly after that.

Here's how I broke down the first report card in Tuesday's issue of Hospitalogy (for a look at some notable spending examples, check out the full article here: https://hihpoint.com/library/6a7e2eac-2208-47e2-adb7-463f19fe7af2)

1. How much has been obligated

So far, states have obligated roughly $4B of the almost $10B awarded across all 50 states for Year One.

2. Pace varies widely by state

10 states had obligated at least 75% of their award by July 31; Georgia, Hawaii, and New Hampshire had committed 100%; and 15 states had obligated less than 10%, including New York and West Virginia at exactly $0. 

Texas, which received the largest Year One award ($281.3M), had obligated just 18.9% ($53.3M), a reminder that award size and obligation pace move independently. 

Six of the slowest states — Alabama, Arkansas, Florida, Idaho, New Mexico, and Wyoming — reported that every obligated dollar so far went to program operations (staffing, administration, grant management) rather than to any of their actual initiatives.

3. Where the money is going

Technology-related categories (IT Advances, Consumer Tech Solutions, and the technology-relevant share of Innovative Care) account for roughly 22% of obligated dollars (about $876M), making technology the single largest theme in Year One spending so far, just ahead of workforce (about $651M, 16%). 

Within the technology bucket, three sub-areas stand out:

• Telehealth and virtual care, approx. $143M obligated, with 20 states reporting activity

• EHR/EMR modernization, approx. $154M obligated, with 15 states reporting activity

• HIE and interoperability, approx. $141M obligated, with 18 states reporting activity

Chronic disease prevention and management (about $481M, 12%) and capital expenditures/infrastructure (about $280M, 7%) round out the largest named categories.

Meaningful obligated dollars also sit under categories like Appropriate Care Availability, Behavioral Health, and Program Administration.

More than half of obligated dollars sit in line items that describe a use rather than naming a recipient type (state agency, contractor, hospital, etc.).

Hospitals show up in some states' line items (38%), but very few name specific hospitals.

4. What's next

Up to $40 billion more is scheduled to flow over the next 4 years of this 5-year, up-to-$50B program. But, per a companion GAO review of CMS's implementation, each state's share depends on demonstrating 'satisfactory progress' toward its approved initiatives, and CMS may withhold, reduce, or recover funding for noncompliance. States have limited ability to appeal those decisions under the program's authorizing legislation.

CMS report PDF: https://www.medicaid.gov/resources-for-states/rural-health/rhtp-resources/RHTP-Obligated-Funds-10082026.pdf

5 Steps to Take Right Now

I have no idea when the bull market that began in March 2013 will end. Market volatility is rising; gains are narrowing; bonds are selling off; domestic politics are bad, and geopolitics are worse.

posts.name: Cullen Roche
posts.text:
I don't think Jake is harsh enough about long-term TIPS. Some people say the 3% real yield on 30 year TIPS is a “guaranteed” high return. This understates the risks:

1) Inflation is personal, not national. TIPS track CPI, not your spending. And in a taxable account you pay tax on the inflation adjustment every year before you get the cash. At 4% inflation and a 24% bracket, that 3% real becomes about 1.3%.

2) The irony of TIPS is they’re the bond most likely to get stiffed in a very high inflation. Rising inflation raises the government’s interest bill when it can least afford it. Argentina didn’t default on its inflation-linked bonds. It just understated inflation for years. Same result. TIPS are supposed to protect you from inflation, but in a high inflation the government has every incentive to make sure they don’t.

3) TIPS lag. They’re indexed to CPI from about three months ago, and the inflation adjustment gets added to principal you don’t receive until maturity. So in a high inflation, when you need the cash most, they aren’t even keeping up in real time.

TIPS are a useful shorter duration matching tool, one of the best. They’re just not a guarantee, certainly not in the long-run. And for most people matching long duration assets to long duration liabilities, equities are usually the better option, in large part because the return premium comes from the lack of a guarantee.

quoted.text:
I think TIPS are very interesting here, but strongly disagree that long-term TIPS have limited risk in real terms... even at 3% real yields. 

1) Over horizons short of their duration, returns are usually dominated by interest-rate moves... the exposure just happens to be to REAL interest rates, but the volatility is still very real. 
2) The result is volatility is just as high in real terms as nominal terms... long-term TIPS have monthly return volatility of ~11–14.5% annualized across 3–10-year periods in nominal or real terms.  
3) They are very tax-inefficient... so hold them in tax-advantaged accounts. In taxable accounts, you can owe federal taxes on both the interest and the inflation adjustment even before receiving that principal. 

Locking in future inflation-adjusted cash flows is valuable, but that doesn’t make the purchasing power of your investment stable if you need to sell along the way.
